title: Matrix Multiplication
description: Master matrix multiplication from its mathematical foundations to efficient NumPy implementations, and understand how it powers linear regression, neural networks, attention mechanisms, and modern AI systems.
learningObjectives: Understand the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication.
Determine when two matrices can be multiplied by checking their dimensions.
Calculate matrix products manually using row-column dot products.
Distinguish matrix multiplication from element-wise multiplication.
Understand the relationship between matrix multiplication and linear transformations.
Understand identity matrices, zero matrices, and matrix powers.
Explain why matrix multiplication is fundamental to neural networks and deep learning.
Recognize numerical, dimensional, and computational considerations when working with matrices.

sections.title: 1. Intuition: Why Do We Need Matrix Multiplication?

content.value: Imagine that you are building an AI system that predicts house prices. Each house has features such as area, number of bedrooms, age, and distance from the city center. A prediction model assigns a weight to each feature and combines the weighted values to produce a prediction.

For a single house, this operation can be expressed as a dot product between its feature vector and the model's weight vector. However, a dataset may contain thousands or millions of houses. Calculating each prediction independently would repeat similar operations many times. Matrix multiplication provides a compact mathematical operation that computes many weighted sums together.
\hat{y}=X\mathbf{w}+b

Here, X is the matrix containing the input features of all observations, w is the weight vector, b is the bias, and y-hat is the vector of predictions. The product Xw calculates a weighted sum for every observation. The bias is then added to each prediction.

The same principle extends to neural networks. Instead of producing one output per observation, a neural network layer may produce hundreds or thousands of output features. Matrix multiplication calculates all these outputs efficiently by combining input activations with learned weights.

Matrix multiplication is therefore more than a mathematical exercise. It is one of the fundamental computational operations behind linear regression, multilayer perceptrons, convolution implementations, transformer architectures, and many other machine learning systems.
Before learning how to multiply matrices, you must understand their dimensions. A matrix with m rows and n columns has shape (m, n). The first number counts rows, while the second counts columns.
A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
For example, a matrix with shape (2, 3) contains two rows and three columns. It has six entries in total. A matrix with shape (3, 4) contains three rows and four columns.
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times3}

The number of rows and columns determines which matrix operations are valid. Matrix multiplication has a specific dimension rule: the number of columns in the first matrix must equal the number of rows in the second matrix.

Suppose A has shape (2, 3) and B has shape (3, 4). The product AB is valid because the first matrix has three columns and the second matrix has three rows. The resulting matrix has two rows and four columns.
(2\times3)(3\times4)=(2\times4)
The inner dimensions must match, and the outer dimensions determine the output shape. This is one of the most important rules in linear algebra for machine learning.

If A has shape (2, 3) and B has shape (2, 4), the product AB is undefined under ordinary matrix multiplication because the inner dimensions, 3 and 2, do not match. You cannot fix this mathematical mismatch by simply changing the output shape.

sections.title: 3. The Mathematical Definition of Matrix Multiplication

content.value: Let A be an m-by-n matrix and B be an n-by-p matrix. Their product C = AB is an m-by-p matrix. Each entry in C is calculated by taking the dot product of one row of A and one column of B.
A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\quad B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p},\quad C=AB\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}
c_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{kj}

The entry c_ij is the element in row i and column j of the output matrix. To calculate it, select row i from A, select column j from B, multiply corresponding elements, and add the products. The index k runs over the shared inner dimension.

Consider the matrices A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. To calculate the entry in the first row and first column of AB, multiply the first row of A by the first column of B. The result is 1 × 5 + 2 × 7 = 19.
The entry in the first row and second column is calculated using the first row of A and the second column of B. Therefore, c_12 = 1 × 6 + 2 × 8 = 22.
Repeating this process for all four output entries gives the complete matrix product. Every output entry is a dot product, which connects matrix multiplication directly to the previous lesson.
Consider the following matrices:
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{bmatrix}
Step 1: Check the dimensions. Both matrices have shape (2, 2), so the product AB is valid and will have shape (2, 2).
Step 2: Calculate the first row of the output. Multiply the first row of A by each column of B.
Step 3: Calculate the second row of the output. Multiply the second row of A by each column of B.
Step 4: Assemble the four entries into the resulting matrix.
AB=\begin{bmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{bmatrix}
The result contains two rows because A has two rows and two columns because B has two columns. The dimensions of the input matrices predict the shape of the result before any arithmetic is performed.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4]
])

B = np.array([
    [5, 6],
    [7, 8]
])

C = A @ B

print("A:\n", A)
print("B:\n", B)
print("AB:\n", C)
print("Output shape:", C.shape)

assert np.array_equal(C, np.array([[19, 22], [43, 50]]))

Matrix multiplication is not restricted to square matrices. In fact, rectangular matrices are especially common in machine learning because the number of input features often differs from the number of output features.
Let A have shape (2, 3) and B have shape (3, 2). The product AB is valid and produces a matrix with shape (2, 2).
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\\5&6\end{bmatrix}
Calculate the first output entry by multiplying the first row of A by the first column of B: 1 × 1 + 2 × 3 + 3 × 5 = 22. The second entry in the first row is 1 × 2 + 2 × 4 + 3 × 6 = 28.
AB=\begin{bmatrix}22&28\\49&64\end{bmatrix}

The output dimensions follow the inner-dimension rule: (2 × 3)(3 × 2) = (2 × 2). A matrix does not need to be square to participate in multiplication. The only requirement is that the shared dimensions match.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6]
])

B = np.array([
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4],
    [5, 6]
])

C = A @ B

print("A shape:", A.shape)
print("B shape:", B.shape)
print("C shape:", C.shape)
print(C)

assert C.shape == (2, 2)

An important consequence is that the product AB and the product BA may have different shapes. If A is (2, 3) and B is (3, 4), AB is valid and has shape (2, 4), but BA is not valid because its inner dimensions would be 4 and 2.

Matrix multiplication and element-wise multiplication are different operations. Matrix multiplication combines rows and columns using dot products. Element-wise multiplication multiplies entries that occupy corresponding positions and produces an array with the same shape when the shapes are equal.
C=AB,\quad c_{ij}=\sum_k a_{ik}b_{kj}
D=A\odot B,\quad d_{ij}=a_{ij}b_{ij}

Consider A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. Matrix multiplication gives [[19, 22], [43, 50]], whereas element-wise multiplication gives [[5, 12], [21, 32]]. The results differ because the operations follow different rules.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])

matrix_product = A @ B
elementwise_product = A * B

print("Matrix multiplication:\n", matrix_product)
print("Element-wise multiplication:\n", elementwise_product)

In NumPy, the @ operator performs matrix multiplication for compatible two-dimensional arrays. The * operator performs element-wise multiplication, subject to broadcasting rules. The np.matmul and np.multiply functions make the distinction explicit.

This distinction is particularly important in deep learning. Dense layers use matrix multiplication to combine features with learned weights, while element-wise multiplication is used in operations such as gating, masks, and certain activation calculations.
Matrix multiplication has several important algebraic properties. Understanding them helps simplify expressions, reason about neural network computations, and detect incorrect assumptions.
Property 1: Associativity. When all required products are defined, changing the grouping of a product of three matrices does not change the mathematical result.
(AB)C=A(BC)

Associativity is useful because it allows us to choose a grouping that reduces computational cost. For example, if multiplying A by B first creates a very large intermediate matrix, multiplying B by C first may be more efficient, provided the dimensions and operation are compatible.
Property 2: Distributivity. Matrix multiplication distributes over matrix addition when the dimensions are compatible.
A(B+C)=AB+AC
Property 3: Scalar compatibility. A scalar factor can be moved between factors in a matrix product, as long as the dimensions are valid.
c(AB)=(cA)B=A(cB)

Property 4: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. In general, AB is not equal to BA. Sometimes both products are defined but yield different matrices; in other cases, only one product is defined.
AB\ne BA\quad\text{in general}
Property 5: The transpose reverses the order of a product.
(AB)^T=B^T A^T

The order reversal is important. Transposing a product does not generally mean transposing each factor while leaving the factors in their original order. The right-hand matrix becomes the left factor after transposition.

These properties are exact mathematical identities. When implemented with floating-point arithmetic, results can differ slightly because different computation orders may introduce different rounding errors.
The identity matrix plays a role similar to the number 1 in ordinary multiplication. Multiplying a compatible matrix by an identity matrix leaves it unchanged.
AI=IA=A
For an n-by-n identity matrix, all diagonal entries are 1 and all off-diagonal entries are 0. The identity matrix maps every vector to itself when used in an ordinary matrix-vector product.
I_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
Identity matrices are useful when defining matrix inverses, expressing transformations, initializing some model parameters, and simplifying mathematical derivations.
A zero matrix contains only zeros. When dimensions are compatible, multiplying a matrix by a zero matrix produces a zero matrix of the appropriate output shape.
A0=0,\quad 0A=0

For example, if A has shape (2, 3) and B is a zero matrix with shape (3, 4), then AB is a zero matrix with shape (2, 4). The output shape is still determined by the matrix multiplication dimension rule.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([
    [2.0, 3.0],
    [4.0, 5.0]
])

I = np.eye(2)
Z = np.zeros((2, 2))

print("A @ I:\n", A @ I)
print("A @ Z:\n", A @ Z)

assert np.allclose(A @ I, A)
assert np.allclose(A @ Z, Z)

For a square matrix A, the matrix power A² means A multiplied by itself: A² = AA. Similarly, A³ = AAA. Matrix powers are defined this way for square matrices because the dimensions must remain compatible for repeated multiplication.
A^2=AA,\quad A^3=AAA

Matrix powers can represent repeated applications of the same linear transformation. If a matrix transforms a state vector once, applying the matrix again transforms the resulting state a second time. This idea appears in dynamical systems, graph algorithms, Markov processes, and recurrent computations.
Consider A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. Its square is [[1, 2], [0, 1]]. Matrix powers accumulate the effect of repeated multiplication; they are not calculated by simply raising each matrix entry to a power.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([
    [1, 1],
    [0, 1]
])

A_squared = A @ A
A_cubed = A @ A @ A

print("A:\n", A)
print("A squared:\n", A_squared)
print("A cubed:\n", A_cubed)
print("Element-wise square:\n", A ** 2)
The expression A ** 2 in NumPy raises each element to the second power. It is not the same as A @ A. Use np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 2) when you specifically need a matrix power.

matrix_square = np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 2)
print(matrix_square)
assert np.array_equal(matrix_square, A @ A)
Matrix-vector multiplication is a special case of matrix multiplication. If A has shape (m, n) and x is a vector with n components, the product Ax is a vector with m components.
A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\quad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad A\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}

Each output component is the dot product of one row of A with the vector x. If A has three rows, the result contains three components. The number of columns in A must equal the number of elements in x.
y_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j
For example, let A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and x = [5, 6]. The first output component is 1 × 5 + 2 × 6 = 17. The second is 3 × 5 + 4 × 6 = 39. Therefore, Ax = [17, 39].

import numpy as np

A = np.array([
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4]
])

x = np.array([5, 6])
y = A @ x

print("Matrix shape:", A.shape)
print("Vector shape:", x.shape)
print("Output:", y)
print("Output shape:", y.shape)

A matrix-vector product is useful when applying a linear transformation to one vector. In machine learning, it can calculate the output of a linear model for one example or transform a representation into a new feature space.

A dense neural network layer transforms input features into output features using a weight matrix and a bias vector. Suppose a batch contains m observations, each with n input features, and the layer has p output units.
X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p},\quad b\in\mathbb{R}^{p}

The layer first calculates XW. The resulting matrix has shape (m, p), with one row per observation and one column per output unit. The bias vector is then added to every row. An activation function may be applied afterward.
Z=XW+b

In this expression, adding b relies on broadcasting in common numerical libraries. The bias has shape (p,), and it is applied to each row of the matrix XW. If the layer uses an activation function such as ReLU, its output becomes max(0, Z) element by element.
\operatorname{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)

The matrix multiplication performs many dot products simultaneously. Each input observation is combined with the weights associated with every output unit. This is why the dot product and matrix multiplication are central to understanding neural network forward propagation.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

batch_size = 4
input_features = 3
output_units = 2

X = rng.normal(size=(batch_size, input_features))
W = rng.normal(size=(input_features, output_units))
b = np.zeros(output_units)

Z = X @ W + b
A = np.maximum(0, Z)

print("Input shape:", X.shape)
print("Weight shape:", W.shape)
print("Bias shape:", b.shape)
print("Pre-activation shape:", Z.shape)
print("Activation shape:", A.shape)

assert Z.shape == (4, 2)

The example uses randomly initialized weights only to demonstrate the computation and dimensions. A trained network learns its weights from data through an optimization procedure such as gradient descent. During training, the matrix multiplication is used in the forward pass, while related matrix operations appear in backpropagation.

Matrix multiplication is also central to transformer models used in language, vision, and multimodal AI. In self-attention, token representations are transformed into query, key, and value matrices. Similarity scores between queries and keys are calculated using matrix multiplication.
S=\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}

Here, Q is the query matrix, K is the key matrix, K-transpose is the transpose of K, and d_k is the key dimension. The product QK-transpose calculates similarity scores between token queries and token keys. Dividing by the square root of d_k scales the scores to help control their magnitude.

The score matrix is passed through a softmax operation, and the resulting weights are used to combine the value matrix V. A common expression for attention is softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)V. The matrix products allow a model to compare multiple tokens and combine their information efficiently.
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V

This equation illustrates why matrix multiplication matters in large language models. Attention involves products between matrices whose dimensions are determined by sequence length, batch size, and feature dimensions. A shape error can make the computation invalid, while a correct shape does not guarantee that the model's mathematical design is appropriate.

Efficient matrix multiplication is a major focus of modern AI hardware. Graphics processing units and specialized accelerators are designed to perform large numbers of multiply-and-accumulate operations in parallel. Efficient kernels, memory layouts, numerical precision, and batching all influence practical performance.

For a straightforward multiplication of an m-by-n matrix and an n-by-p matrix, the classical algorithm performs approximately mnp scalar multiplications and a similar order of additions. Its arithmetic complexity is O(mnp).
T(m,n,p)=O(mnp)

For two square n-by-n matrices, the classical algorithm therefore requires O(n³) arithmetic operations. Advanced algorithms can improve the theoretical complexity, but highly optimized classical matrix multiplication remains widely used because of its practical efficiency and hardware support.

Memory is another important consideration. An m-by-n matrix stores mn elements. If each element uses four bytes, a matrix containing 10 million elements requires approximately 40 million bytes, or about 40 MB using decimal units, before accounting for temporary arrays and additional model state.

Floating-point calculations are approximate. Multiplication and addition may introduce rounding errors, especially when values differ greatly in magnitude or when many operations are accumulated. Mathematical identities should therefore be tested using tolerances when comparing floating-point results.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.1, 0.2], [0.3, 0.4]], dtype=np.float64)
B = np.array([[0.5, 0.6], [0.7, 0.8]], dtype=np.float64)

C = A @ B
print(C)

expected = np.array([
    [0.19, 0.22],
    [0.43, 0.50]
])

print("Approximately correct:", np.allclose(C, expected))
assert np.allclose(C, expected)

The allclose function compares values using numerical tolerances. It is usually more appropriate than exact equality for results produced by floating-point computations. The tolerances should be chosen according to the numerical requirements of the application.
Mistake 1: Forgetting the inner-dimension rule. A matrix with shape (m, n) can multiply a matrix with shape (n, p), producing shape (m, p).
Mistake 2: Assuming the output has the same shape as the first matrix. The output has the row count of the first matrix and the column count of the second matrix.
Mistake 3: Assuming AB equals BA. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. Check both the dimensions and the actual mathematical values before making such a claim.
Mistake 4: Confusing A @ B with A * B in NumPy. The former performs matrix multiplication for compatible matrices, while the latter performs element-wise multiplication with broadcasting.
Mistake 5: Treating A ** 2 as a matrix square. In NumPy, exponentiation is applied element by element. Use A @ A or np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 2) for a matrix square.
Mistake 6: Assuming a mathematically valid product is automatically semantically meaningful. The axes and feature meanings must be consistent with the problem being modeled.
Mistake 7: Using exact equality to test floating-point results. Use np.allclose or np.isclose where small numerical differences are expected.

Mistake 8: Ignoring intermediate memory requirements. A valid matrix product may still be too expensive if it creates a very large intermediate matrix. Computational planning can matter as much as mathematical validity.

sections.title: 15. Mini Project: Build a Simple Dense Neural Network Layer

content.value: Implement a simple dense layer from scratch using NumPy. Generate a batch of input observations, initialize a weight matrix and bias vector, calculate the linear transformation, apply ReLU, and verify the output dimensions. The purpose is to understand the forward computation rather than train a complete network.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# Configuration
batch_size = 8
input_dim = 5
hidden_dim = 4
output_dim = 2

# Example inputs
X = rng.normal(size=(batch_size, input_dim))

# Parameters for the first dense layer
W1 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, size=(input_dim, hidden_dim))
b1 = np.zeros(hidden_dim)

# Parameters for the output layer
W2 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, size=(hidden_dim, output_dim))
b2 = np.zeros(output_dim)

# Forward pass
Z1 = X @ W1 + b1
A1 = np.maximum(0, Z1)
Z2 = A1 @ W2 + b2

print("X:", X.shape)
print("W1:", W1.shape)
print("Z1:", Z1.shape)
print("A1:", A1.shape)
print("W2:", W2.shape)
print("Z2:", Z2.shape)

assert X.shape == (8, 5)
assert Z1.shape == (8, 4)
assert A1.shape == (8, 4)
assert Z2.shape == (8, 2)

print("Output predictions:\n", Z2)

The first matrix product transforms five input features into four hidden features. The second product transforms those four hidden features into two output values. The batch dimension remains eight throughout the network because every input observation produces one corresponding output row.

The weights and biases are randomly initialized and have not been trained. To extend the project, define a target matrix, calculate a loss such as mean squared error, derive gradients using calculus, and update the parameters with gradient descent. Those steps connect matrix multiplication to the optimization concepts introduced later in this module.

exercises.question: Matrix A has shape (4, 3), and matrix B has shape (3, 5). Is AB valid? If so, what is the shape of the output?
hints: Compare the number of columns in A with the number of rows in B.
The output uses the outer dimensions.
exercises.solution: Yes. The inner dimensions are both 3, so multiplication is valid. The output shape is (4, 5).

exercises.question: Calculate AB for A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]]. Show the calculation for each output entry.
hints: Each output entry is the dot product of a row of A and a column of B.

exercises.question: Explain the difference between matrix multiplication and element-wise multiplication. How do you express each operation in NumPy?
exercises.solution: Matrix multiplication calculates output entries using row-column dot products. Element-wise multiplication multiplies corresponding entries. In NumPy, A @ B performs matrix multiplication for compatible two-dimensional arrays, while A * B performs element-wise multiplication subject to broadcasting rules.

exercises.question: Create a matrix with shape (3, 4) and another matrix with shape (4, 2). Multiply them using NumPy and verify that the output shape is (3, 2).
hints: Use np.arange or np.random.default_rng to create the arrays.
Use an assertion to verify the output shape.
exercises.solution:
import numpy as np

A = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
B = np.arange(8).reshape(4, 2)
C = A @ B

print(C)
print(C.shape)
assert C.shape == (3, 2)

exercises.question: A neural network receives a batch of 64 examples with 20 features each. A dense layer contains 12 output units. Determine the shapes of the input, weight matrix, bias vector, and output. Explain why the batch dimension remains unchanged.
hints: The weight matrix maps 20 input features to 12 output units.
exercises.solution: The input shape is (64, 20). The weight matrix shape is (20, 12). The bias vector shape is (12,). The output shape is (64, 12). Matrix multiplication transforms each input row independently using the same weights, so the number of observations remains 64.

exercises.question: Explain why (AB)C = A(BC) can be true even though AB generally does not equal BA. Distinguish associativity from commutativity.
exercises.solution: Associativity states that changing the grouping of compatible matrix products does not change their mathematical result: (AB)C = A(BC). Commutativity would state that swapping the order does not change the result: AB = BA. Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.

exercises.question: Implement a function that checks whether two two-dimensional NumPy arrays can be multiplied using ordinary matrix multiplication. If they can, return their product; otherwise, raise a ValueError containing both input shapes.
hints: Check that both inputs have exactly two dimensions.
